notes.meaning: The disciples had been arguing about who would get the top place. They pictured an earthly kingdom with high posts to hand out. Jesus had just told them He would suffer and die, yet they fixed on glory instead. Many people love to hear about rewards but pass over the hard work and the cross.

Jesus answered with a living picture. He called a little child, old enough to walk to Him, and stood him in the middle of the group. The child was there not to play with, but to learn from. A later story says this child grew up to be Ignatius, an early church leader, but commentators call that story unreliable.

To "change" here means to turn around, or repent. The disciples were heading the wrong way with their pride and ambition. They must become like little children, who don't chase rank and are humble and teachable. Without this they would not even get into the kingdom, let alone be great in it. Jesus was not saying children are without sin. He meant only that we must drop our pride as they do.

differ.view: Wesley adds that every person must be fully changed inside, made new in God's image, in this life to enter heaven. He admits this verse alone may not say that much.
Barnes says the word means the disciples had to change their wrong ideas about Jesus' kingdom. It does not by itself mean they were not yet believers.

notes.meaning: Here is Jesus' surprising answer to their question: the humblest person is the greatest. Humility means seeing yourself as you really are. A humble person claims no merit before God and does not look down on others. Such people are most like Christ.

The "little child" now stands for any humble believer. When we welcome and help such a person for Jesus' sake, Jesus counts it as done to Himself. This looks ahead to His words in Matthew 25:40 about serving "the least of these."

To cause someone to "stumble" means to lead them into sin or block their faith. The "little ones" are believers of any age who trust like children. The millstone was a huge stone turned by a donkey. Being drowned with one was a punishment for the worst criminals. Jesus says even that would be better than harming His humble followers. This is also a comfort to believers whom the world looks down on.

Things that cause people to stumble are sure to come. The world is sinful and Satan is crafty. The first "woe" is sorrow for the harm this does to the world. The second is a warning to the one who causes it. The fact that such things must come is no excuse for the person who brings them.

differ.view: Calvin says it is God's will to leave His people facing stumbling blocks. This tests their faith and separates true believers from false ones.
Wesley and Clarke stress that stumbling blocks come because of people's weakness and stubborn wickedness. Both the one who causes the stumbling and the one who falls are in danger.

notes.meaning: Jesus is not asking us to hurt our bodies. He uses a strong picture to make His point. Whatever leads you into sin must go, even if it is as dear to you as a hand or an eye. That may be a habit, a pleasure, or a close friendship. It is better to enter life without it than to keep it and be lost in the fire of hell.

Never look down on even the weakest believer. God's angels care for them, and those same angels stand near God's throne. They are like trusted officials who are allowed to see the king's face. So it is a serious thing to scorn people whom heaven watches over.

differ.view: Adam Clarke believes this verse teaches that each person has a guardian angel of their own.
Calvin says the verse doesn't teach one angel per person. Many angels together guard each believer as needed.

notes.meaning: This verse is in the King James Version but not in the oldest manuscripts. The same words do appear in Luke 19:10. They give another reason not to despise humble believers: Jesus came to seek and save the lost. If He valued them that much, we should not treat them as worthless.

A good shepherd will leave the rest of the flock to look for one lost sheep. He is full of joy when he finds it. In this chapter the picture shows how much God cares for each believer who wanders. It also shows how unwilling He is to lose even one. So we too should gently bring wanderers back, not drive them away.

The Father does not want even one of these little ones to be lost. Notice the steps in this passage: the angels serve them, the Son came to save them, and the Father Himself cares for them. Anyone who makes them stumble is working against God's will.

differ.view: Barnes says this shows believers are safe. No one can snatch them out of God's hand.
Clarke says that if anyone is finally lost, it is not because God willed it. It is because they chose darkness over light.

notes.meaning: When a fellow believer wrongs you, don't complain about it to others. Go to them alone and kindly show them the wrong. Often a quiet talk clears it up. The goal is to win your brother back, not to get even.

If they won't listen, don't give up. Take one or two others along. They can help you reason with the person and give your words more weight. They can also be witnesses if the matter goes further. This follows the law in Deuteronomy 19:15.

If they still refuse, bring it to the church: either the local congregation or its leaders. If they won't listen even to the church, treat them as an outsider. That means no longer treating them as a fellow church member. You still owe them kindness, and the hope is always that they will turn back.

What Jesus said to Peter in 16:19 He now says to all the disciples. When the church acts on Christ's word in correcting its members, heaven stands behind it. That includes putting out someone who refuses to repent and welcoming back someone who does. This is a warning to the stubborn and a comfort to the repentant.

differ.view: Spurgeon taught that each local congregation holds the keys of its own door. Heaven confirms what it rightly does.
Calvin says this oversight is given to the church's elders. Heaven backs their decisions only when they follow God's word.
Clarke, following an older scholar, says "bind" and "loose" were Jewish teachers' words for declaring what is forbidden and what is allowed.

notes.meaning: God gives special honor to believers who pray together with one heart. The word "agree" is like instruments playing in tune. In this setting the promise especially covers prayer about church discipline. It also encourages joint prayer of every kind.

differ.view: Barnes taught that this promise was given to the apostles as they set up the church. He did not apply it to everyday prayers.
Guzik teaches that agreeing together in prayer has a great, multiplying power.

notes.meaning: Even if only two or three meet in Jesus' name, He is with them by His Spirit. Meeting "in His name" means gathering to worship Him and follow His word. Numbers don't matter; faith does. Only God could promise to be present in every gathering at once, so this shows that Jesus is God.
Peter knew he must forgive. But he wanted to know where the limit was. Jewish teachers said to forgive three times, so Peter thought seven was generous. Our hearts like to set limits on doing good.
Jesus' number can be read as seventy-seven or as 490. Either way He means there is no limit. We should forgive as often as needed and not keep count of wrongs done to us.

Jesus tells a parable, a story with a lesson, to show why we must forgive. The king stands for God, who will one day settle accounts with each of us. The "servants" were probably high officials, such as tax collectors for the king.
Ten thousand talents was a huge fortune, far more than any servant could ever repay. It pictures how great our debt of sin is toward God, and how unable we are to pay it.

In those days a creditor could sell a debtor and his family into slavery. The scene shows what our sin deserves if God dealt with us by strict justice. Barnes notes that the detail about the family is part of the story. It does not mean God punishes children for a father's sin.

The servant bowed low and begged. This was humble pleading, not religious worship. He asked for more time and promised to pay it all, which he never could. Henry says it is foolish to think we can repay God for our sins ourselves.

The master was moved with pity. He gave far more than the servant asked: he cancelled the whole debt and set him free. This pictures God's tender mercy, which forgives even the greatest sins of those who humbly come to Him.

A hundred denarii was a small sum next to ten thousand talents. Yet the forgiven servant grabbed his fellow servant by the throat. The point is that wrongs others do to us are small compared with our wrongs against God.
The fellow servant used the same posture and nearly the same words that had won mercy for the first servant. He should have known exactly how that man felt.
He flatly and stubbornly refused, and had the man jailed. Even the other servants saw how shameful this was from someone who had just been shown such mercy.

The other servants were grieved and told their master everything. Henry draws a lesson: bring your sorrow over wrongs to God in prayer and leave it with Him. Barnes warns that this is a story detail. It does not mean God needs us to tell Him what happens.

The master calls the servant wicked, because refusing mercy is a real sin. He reminds him how much he had been forgiven. Those who have received mercy should show mercy. Knowing how much God has forgiven us helps us forgive others.

The angry master handed him over to harsh punishment until he paid it all. He could never pay so vast a debt, so there was no hope of release. Calvin and Robertson say this points to eternal judgment, not a time of cleansing after death.

Here is the lesson. God will deal this way with those who will not forgive. Forgiving "from the heart" means more than words. It means holding no grudge, wanting no revenge, and even seeking the good of the one who hurt you.

differ.view: Matthew Henry says God does not take back a real pardon. The story exposes people who only thought they were forgiven but never truly knew God's grace.
MacArthur says Jesus is speaking to true believers. An unforgiving heart brings God's loving discipline, not the loss of salvation.
